lesson.title: Why test a hypothesis?
lesson.lead: A sample is a small, lucky-or-unlucky glimpse. Testing asks how likely that glimpse would be if the claim were true.

blocks.text: A tyre maker claims the **average life is 50,000 km**. You cannot test every tyre, so you take 30 at random and get a mean of **47,000 km** (s = 5,500 km). Is the claim false, or were you unlucky?

items: Assume the claim is true (μ = 50,000).
Ask: if so, how probable is a sample mean of 47,000 or lower? Here that is about 0.0013 (a tiny tail area).
So either you drew a very unusual sample, or the claim is probably false. The smaller the probability, the more doubt you have.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: More data makes the argument stronger. Getting a low average from 30 tyres is unlikely; getting it from 100 tyres is far less likely. He also stressed that every statement comes with an error bound: "I am wrong at most 2.5% of the time" beats "I think so".
Why bother

items: **Validate an assumption** about a process or population
**Support a decision** with data instead of a hunch
**Judge significance:** is the effect real, or just chance? (Five heads in a row: possible with a fair coin, probability 1/32.)

blocks.text: Parametric or not

A **parametric** test assumes the data follow a known distribution (normal, t, χ²), so errors can be written as areas under a curve. **Non-parametric** tests assume no distribution, so they cannot give such error statements. This course uses parametric tests.

lesson.title: H₀ and H₁: who gets the equals sign
lesson.lead: The null always contains the equality. The alternative is the strict opposite.

head: H₀ (null)
H₁ (alternative)
rows: No difference, or a difference due to sampling variation
The difference you are trying to establish
What we conclude if H₀ is rejected

blocks.text: The three examples from class

head: Statement
H₀
H₁
Who owns the claim?
rows: Dealership: oil change is less than 15 min

blocks.text: Notice that the claim can be either hypothesis. Look at the symbol, not at who said it: if the claim contains = (or ≤, ≥), it is H₀; if it is strict (<, >), it is H₁.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: The tail comes from H₁. **<** means left-tailed, **>** means right-tailed, **≠** means two-tailed. Words like "significantly different" mean two-tailed; "more than" and "at least" point you to the sign.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: When H₀ is a range such as μ ≥ K, the test statistic still uses the single value μ = K. Board 6 explains why.

lesson.title: Two ways to be wrong
lesson.lead: Every decision can be wrong in exactly two ways. α controls one of them.

blocks.text: α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true)      β = P(do not reject H₀ | H₀ false)
**Level of significance α** is the largest Type I error you will accept. Pushing the cut-off further into the tail lowers α but makes Type II errors more likely: you cannot shrink both for free.
The courtroom

H₀: the defendant is innocent. With heavy evidence the jury **rejects H₀** (guilty). With weak evidence the verdict is **not guilty**, which only says the evidence was not enough. It does not say innocent.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: This is a one-way test. **Reject H₀** is a strong statement. **Fail to reject H₀** only means there is insufficient evidence. In the exam, write "do not reject H₀", never "accept H₀" (several slide solutions say "accept", but the careful wording is "fail to reject").

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Never write "H₀ is proved" or "H₁ is proved". Write: "At the 5% level there is (not) enough evidence to conclude …" and finish with the answer in plain words.

lesson.title: α, p-values and tails
lesson.lead: Two roads to the same verdict: the critical value, and the p-value.

blocks.text: **α** is fixed by you before seeing the data: it defines the rejection region. The **p-value** belongs to your sample: it is the probability, if H₀ is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one you got.
p ≤ α  ⇒  reject H₀            p > α  ⇒  do not reject H₀

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: A p-value of 0.0005 is far stronger evidence than 0.01. The smaller p is, the less likely your sample would be under H₀, so the more safely you can reject.
Critical z values
In a two-tailed test α is **split in half**, α/2 in each tail. That pushes the cut-offs outwards (1.645 becomes 1.96 at 5%; 2.33 becomes 2.58 at 1%).

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: For a two-tailed test the p-value is **twice** the one-tail area. Compare 2 × (tail area) with α, or compare |z| with z_{α/2}. Do not mix: using a one-tail critical value with a two-tail p-value flips decisions near the boundary.
Left, right or two-tailed: what to do

head: Left-tailed (H₁: μ < K)
Right-tailed (H₁: μ > K)
Two-tailed (H₁: μ ≠ K)
rows: search 1 − α, then put a minus sign

blocks.text: Check the direction first. If the sample mean moved the opposite way to H₁ (for example H₁: μ > K but x̄ is below K), z is on the wrong side, p is bigger than 0.5, and you cannot reject. No table needed.
Reading the exam z-table (area to the LEFT)

The May 2026 paper prints the **cumulative standard normal table**: "Table values represent AREA to the LEFT of the Z score". The **edges** (left column and top row) are z-values. The **inside** numbers are areas, between 0.5 and about 0.9936 (z up to 2.49). Negative z is not printed, so use symmetry.

items: **z to p-value:** split z (1.84 = row 1.8 + column 0.04), read the area inside (0.96712), then p = 1 − 0.96712 = 0.033. Double it for a two-tailed test.

**α to cut-off:** work out the left area (1 − α, or 1 − α/2 for two tails), search for it **inside** the table, and read z from the edges. For 0.95 you find 0.94950 (z = 1.64) and 0.95053 (z = 1.65), so the cut-off is 1.645.
**Add the sign from H₁:** ">" gives plus, "<" gives minus, "≠" gives both. The table never decides the sign.
**Negative z:** the left area for −z is 1 − (area for +z), and the tail is the same size as for +z.
**z beyond 2.49:** read the cut-off from the bottom z row of the t-table instead (1.282, 1.645, 1.960, 2.326, 2.576).

blocks.label: Common mix-up
blocks.text: Searching 0.95 on the edges instead of inside the table gives 0.82894, which is the area for z = 0.95. That is not the cut-off. Areas live inside the table and z lives on the edges.
Every case: from z to the p-value
Φ(z) means the number you read from the left-area table for |z|. Always look up |z|, since the table has no negative z.
Every case: from α to the cut-off
Cut-off and p-value: two directions through the same table

head: You start with
You end with
Where the "1 −" comes
Steps
rows: 1 − α, then search that number inside the table, then read z from the edges
look up |z| to get the area, then p = 1 − area

blocks.text: The table only gives the area to the **left**. The tail we care about is the small leftover piece on the end, and "1 −" is how you reach it. For the cut-off you need the area *up to* the cut-off, which is 1 − α. For p you have the area *up to* |z| and want what is left beyond it, which is 1 − area. The two are mirror images of each other.

blocks.label: Sign versus size
blocks.text: The **sign** of z and of the cut-off shows direction: negative means left, positive means right. **p is a probability**, so it is always between 0 and 1 and never negative. The sign comes from the data and H₁. The "1 −" comes from using a left-area table.

blocks.label: Two exceptions
blocks.text: (1) If z is on the **wrong side** of what H₁ points to, p = Φ(|z|) with no "1 −". It comes out above 0.5 and you do not reject. (2) For a **two-tailed** test, compute 1 − Φ(|z|) and then double it.
Special cases

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The tail is tiny, p is under 0.007. For cut-offs like ±2.58, use the bottom z row of the t-table.
Look up the positive version, then apply the rules above.
Sample on the wrong side of H₁
Do not reject. No lookup needed.
Use the t-table: row by df, column by α, one-tail or two-tail.

blocks.text: Reject H₀ if p ≤ α, or if z is beyond the cut-off in the direction of H₁'s arrow. Otherwise: do not reject H₀.

lesson.title: The test statistic, and why μ = K
lesson.lead: Every test is signal ÷ noise. The only thing that changes between tests is the noise recipe.

blocks.text: statistic = (what the sample shows − what H₀ says) ÷ standard error
If H₀ is true, the sample mean x̄ is itself roughly normal, with mean μ₀ and standard deviation σ/√n. Standardising gives the familiar statistic:
When σ is unknown, replace it by the sample SD s. The statistic then follows a **t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom**; for large n, t is almost the same as z.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: The denominator s/√n is the SD of the **sample mean**. s alone is the SD of individual observations. (A student asked about exactly this in class.)
Why use the boundary value μ = K? (not on the slides)
Say H₀ is μ ≥ K, a whole range of possible means, but the formula needs one number. The cut-off z_α is placed using μ = K, the edge of the range.

items: With μ = K, the chance of landing below the cut-off is exactly α.
If the true mean is larger than K, the whole curve slides right, so less probability lies below the same cut-off: the error falls **below** α.
So for every mean allowed by H₀ the Type I error is **at most α**. That is the guarantee practitioners want ("at most 5%", never "at least").

blocks.text: Numbers: left-tailed test at 5%, cut-off −1.645. If the true mean sits one standard error above K, the chance of a false rejection is Φ(−1.645 − 1) = **0.004**, far below 0.05. Centring the test anywhere below K could let the error exceed α.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: He said this was not in the slides because it is a doubt you will certainly have, and that his OneNote notes would be uploaded.

lesson.title: Tests for one mean (z and t)
lesson.lead: Same five steps every time. Pick z or t from what you know about σ and n.

items: Write H₀ and H₁ (this fixes the tail).
Choose α.
Compute the statistic with the boundary value μ₀.
Compare with the critical value, or compute the p-value.
Write the verdict in one plain sentence.

head: Use
When
rows: σ known, or n ≥ 30 (then s can stand in for σ)

blocks.text: Slide 35 adds that for σ unknown and n ≥ 30, t is technically more accurate but z is acceptable because they are close.
Worked in class: sodium
Claim: mean sodium **no more than 920 mg**. n = 44, x̄ = 925, s = 18, α = 0.05. H₀: μ ≤ 920 vs H₁: μ > 920. z = (925 − 920)/(18/√44) = **1.84 > 1.645**, so reject: the claim is doubtful.
Play with the numbers (his advice)
Bigger s means more noise, so a weaker signal. Bigger n cuts the noise, but only by √n.

blocks.label: Check the numbers
blocks.text: In the recording he suggested that n = 440 with s = 180 would give about the same z as before. Working it out gives 0.58, not 1.84. Ten times the sample size cuts noise by √10 ≈ 3.2, so s could only grow to about 57 to keep z near 1.84. The idea (more data can offset noise) is right; just don't copy those numbers.
Two-tailed example: delivery time
Company claims a mean of 3 days. n = 50, x̄ = 3.4, σ = 1.2. "Significantly different" so two-tailed: z = 0.4/(1.2/√50) = **2.36 > 1.96**, reject.

lesson.title: Comparing two means
lesson.lead: Variances of independent sample means add, so the noise is √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

blocks.text: z = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂)

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: Why the variances add: x̄₁ and x̄₂ are independent normal variables, and the variance of their difference is the sum of their variances. If the σ's are unknown, use s₁ and s₂ (large samples).
**Small samples:** use the pooled t-test, with df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
s_p² = [(n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²] / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)      t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / (s_p √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂))
Taxi tyres (class)

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide prints z = 2.30; recomputing gives 2.37. The decision (reject) is the same either way, so don't lose sleep, but show your own working in the exam.

blocks.label: Paired or unpaired?
blocks.text: Ask: does the same person or item appear in both sets? If yes (before and after, same subjects), it is **paired**: work on the differences, df = pairs − 1. If the two groups are different people, it is **unpaired**: pooled t, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
Paired data

If the **same subjects** are measured twice (before and after), take the differences d and do a one-sample t-test on d with df = n − 1. Treating paired data as two independent samples throws away information.

lesson.title: Proportion tests
lesson.lead: A proportion is just a mean of 0s and 1s, so the same recipe works with a different standard error.

blocks.text: Let each person be Xᵢ = 1 (has the characteristic, probability P) or 0 (probability 1 − P). Then E(Xᵢ) = P and Var(Xᵢ) = P − P² = **PQ**. The sample proportion is the average, so its variance is PQ/n.
z = (p̂ − P₀) / √(P₀Q₀/n)

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: The exact standard deviation carries a finite-population factor √((N − n)/(N − 1)), because sampling is done without replacement. If n is small compared with N the factor is almost 1 and is dropped. Under H₀, use P₀ (not p̂) in the denominator.
Disease survival (class)
20 patients, 18 survived: p̂ = 0.90. H₀: P = 0.85, H₁: P > 0.85, α = 0.05. z = 0.05/√(0.85×0.15/20) = **0.63 < 1.645**, so do not reject: not enough evidence that survival exceeds 85%.
Two proportions (the two judges)
Judge 1: 90 false positives in 3,000 (3.00%). Judge 2: 48 in 2,500 (1.92%). H₀: P₁ = P₂ vs H₁: P₁ > P₂.

**Why pooled?** The test assumes H₀ is true, and H₀ says both groups share one proportion, so the best single estimate pools the data. The unpooled form √(p̂₁q̂₁/n₁ + p̂₂q̂₂/n₂) gives z = 2.60 here, the same decision. Unpooled is the natural choice for a confidence interval for P₁ − P₂, where no H₀ is assumed.

blocks.label: Open item
blocks.text: In class the professor thought the pooled p*q* looked wrong and said he would verify it next lecture. Use pooled when H₀: P₁ = P₂ (the Feb 2026 answer key does).

lesson.title: The t-test and the F-test
lesson.lead: For small samples with σ unknown. (Left for the next class, but asked in exams.)

blocks.text: The t curve is bell-shaped like z but with fatter tails; the fewer degrees of freedom, the fatter the tails. So the critical value is larger than z's: at 5% one-tailed, t(9) = 1.833, t(23) = 1.714, t(30) = 1.697, closing in on z's 1.645 as df grows.
One mean (slide 36)

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The sample mean is **below** the claim. A right-tailed test (H₁: μ > 18,580) can never reject here, because t is negative (p = 0.96). The slide compares |t| = 1.929 with 1.833 and rejects, which only makes sense for H₁: μ < 18,580 (left-tailed, p = 0.043, reject at 5% but not at 1% where the cut-off is 2.821). Always check the **sign** against H₁.
Two means, small samples (slide 41)

Courier packets: 15 at month start (x̄ = 5.25, s² = 1.20), 10 at month end (x̄ = 4.26, s² = 1.15). Pooled s_p² = 1.180, SE = 0.4436, t = 0.99/0.4436 = **2.23**, df = 23. "Heavier at the start" is one-tailed: critical 1.714, so reject; p = 0.018. The 95% CI for μ₁ − μ₂ is 0.99 ± 2.069 × 0.4436 = (0.07, 1.91).

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide uses the two-tailed cut-off 2.069 with H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂, yet the question asks "heavier" (one-tailed) and quotes a one-tailed p-value (0.01 to 0.025). Decide the tail from the question text.
Paired (slide 43)

9 trainees, differences d = after − before: −5, 7, 11, −8, 11, 21, 0, 9, −1. d̄ = 5, s_d = 9.21, t = 5/(9.21/3) = **1.63**, df = 8. One-tailed 5% critical value is **1.860**, two-tailed 2.306: fail to reject either way.

blocks.label: Slide check
blocks.text: The slide uses 1.833, which is the df = 9 value. With 9 pairs, df = n − 1 = 8, so the critical value is 1.860. Count df from the number of **pairs**.
F-test for two variances (not in the slides, asked in Sep 2025)
F = s₁²/s₂²   with df (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1)      H₁: σ₁² > σ₂² is right-tailed

Sep 2025: s₁ = 0.032 (n = 10), s₂ = 0.028 (n = 14). F = 1.306 against F₀.₀₅(9, 13) = 2.714, so there is no evidence that method A is more variable. The Hypothesis Testing guide (pp. 21 to 22) covers it.

lesson.title: Chi-square tests
lesson.lead: For counts in categories. Compare what you observed with what H₀ predicts.

blocks.text: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E        (always a right-tailed test)

items: Use **frequencies only**, never percentages, means or proportions.
Variables are categorical; the test shows **association**, not cause.
Check that every expected count is **at least 5**; otherwise merge categories (or use an exact test).

blocks.text: Independence (r × c table)
H₀: the two variables are independent. Expected count E = (row total × column total) / N. Degrees of freedom = **(r − 1)(c − 1)**.
Accident timing vs fatality (slide 51): E = 69.3, 210.7, 29.7, 90.3, χ² = **7.32**, df = 1, critical 3.841, reject: timing and outcome are associated.
Smoking vs hypertension (2 × 3): χ² = **14.46**, df = 2, critical 5.991, reject.
Goodness of fit
H₀: the data follow a stated distribution. df = **k − 1 − m**, where k is the number of categories and m the number of parameters estimated from the data.

Digits in a phone directory, expected 1,000 each (as on the slide): χ² = **59.4**, df = 9, critical 16.919, reject uniformity. (The slide prints 58.54; recomputing gives 59.36. The listed counts actually add to 9,990, not 10,000. Same decision.)
Bus arrivals vs Poisson: λ = 2.96 was **estimated**, so df = 6 − 1 − 1 = **4**. χ² = 11.75 < 13.28 (α = 0.01), so a Poisson model is acceptable.

blocks.label: Spot it
blocks.text: Exercise 10 (slide 71): insurance type vs hospital stay has an expected count of 25×10/70 = **3.57 < 5**, so the χ² test should not be applied as it stands. That is the answer being looked for.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Do not forget to subtract estimated parameters from the df in goodness-of-fit tests.

lesson.title: Which test do I use?
lesson.lead: Exams reward picking the right test in 30 seconds. Ask three questions.

blocks.text: **1. What did you measure?** Numbers (times, weights) or yes/no and categories?   **2. How many groups?**   **3. If two groups: the same subjects twice, or different subjects?**

worked.title: Sodium in a sandwich (z, one mean)

problem.text: A restaurant says its breakfast sandwich has **no more than 920 mg** of sodium. A random sample of 44 has mean 925 mg and s = 18 mg. At α = 0.05, is there enough evidence to reject the claim?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ ≤ 920 (the claim, contains ≤). H₁: μ > 920. The sign in H₁ makes it **right-tailed**.

steps.label: Which test
steps.text: n = 44 ≥ 30, so z is fine, and s stands in for σ.

steps.label: Statistic
steps.text: SE = s/√n = 18/√44 = 2.714. z = (925 − 920)/2.714 = **1.84**. (Use μ = 920, the boundary, even though H₀ is a range.)

steps.label: Plain English
steps.text: At the 5% level there is enough evidence that the mean sodium exceeds 920 mg, so the restaurant's claim is doubtful.

worked.answer: z = 1.84 > 1.645: reject H₀; the claim of at most 920 mg is doubtful.

worked.title: Light bulbs (left-tailed z, α = 1%)

problem.text: A manufacturer guarantees the mean life of a bulb is **not less than 750 hours**. A random sample of 36 bulbs has mean 745 hours and s = 60 hours. At the 1% level, is there enough evidence to reject the claim?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ ≥ 750 (the claim). H₁: μ < 750. The "<" sign makes it **left-tailed**.

steps.label: Which test
steps.text: n = 36 ≥ 30, so z is fine (s stands in for σ). α = 0.01.

steps.label: Critical value
steps.text: Search 1 − 0.01 = 0.99 inside the table: 0.99010 at z = 2.33. Left-tailed, so the cut-off is **−2.33**.

steps.label: p-value
steps.text: Table area for 0.5 is 0.69146, so p = 1 − 0.69146 = **0.31**, far above 0.01.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: −0.5 is not below −2.33 (equivalently p = 0.31 > 0.01): **do not reject H₀**. Say "do not reject", not "accept".

steps.label: Plain English
steps.text: At the 1% level there is not enough evidence that the mean life is below 750 hours. The 5-hour gap is small next to the noise of 10 hours.

worked.answer: z = −0.5 > −2.33: do not reject H₀; the claim of at least 750 hours stands.

worked.title: Textbook Ex. 9 (left-tailed z), walked line by line

problem.text: Anderson, Sweeney and Williams, Chapter 9, Exercise 9. H₀: μ ≥ 20 and H₁: μ < 20. A sample of 50 gives x̄ = 19.4, and the population standard deviation is 2. (a) Find the test statistic. (b) Find the p-value. (c) Conclude at α = 0.05. (d) Give the rejection rule using the critical value and conclude.

steps.label: Setup
steps.text: H₁ has "<", so the test is **left-tailed** and the cut-off is negative. σ is given, so use **z**. Direction check: x̄ = 19.4 is below 20, which matches the arrow, so go on.

steps.label: (b) p-value
steps.text: Look up |z| = 2.12 (row 2.1, column 0.02): 0.98300. Left-tailed with z negative, so p = 1 − 0.98300 = **0.017**.

steps.label: (c) Conclusion
steps.text: p = 0.017 ≤ 0.05, so **reject H₀**. There is evidence that the mean is below 20.

steps.label: (d) Critical value
steps.text: Left-tailed at 5%: search 1 − 0.05 = 0.95 inside the table to get 1.645, then add the minus sign. Rule: reject if z ≤ −1.645. Here −2.12 ≤ −1.645, so **reject H₀**.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Parts (c) and (d) must agree. If they do not, look for an arithmetic or sign slip.

worked.answer: z = −2.12, p = 0.017, cut-off −1.645: reject H₀ at 5%.

worked.title: Delivery time (two-tailed z)

problem.text: A company claims an average delivery time of 3 days. A watchdog samples 50 deliveries: mean 3.4 days, σ = 1.2 days. At α = 0.05, is the average **significantly different** from 3?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ = 3, H₁: μ ≠ 3. "Different" in either direction means **two-tailed**.

steps.label: Critical values
steps.text: Two-tailed 5% splits into 2.5% per tail. Search 1 − 0.025 = 0.975 inside the table (row 1.9, column 0.06): cut-offs **±1.96**. p-value: table area for 2.36 is 0.99086, so one tail = 0.00914 and p = 2 × 0.00914 = **0.018**.

worked.answer: z = 2.36, beyond ±1.96: the mean delivery time is significantly different from 3 days.

worked.title: Taxi tyres (two-sample z)

problem.text: Brand A: n = 30, mean 38,600 km, s = 5,000. Brand B: n = 40, mean 35,450 km, s = 6,100. Test at 5% whether the brands differ.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂, H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (two-tailed).

steps.label: Note
steps.text: The slide shows 2.30; the arithmetic gives 2.37. Same decision.

worked.answer: z = 2.37 > 1.96: the two brands do not have equal mean life.

worked.title: Disease survival (one proportion)

problem.text: Of 20 people who caught a disease, 18 survived. At α = 0.05, test H₀: survival rate = 85% against the alternative that it is higher.

steps.label: Plain English
steps.text: With only 20 patients the sample does not give enough evidence that survival exceeds 85%.

worked.answer: z = 0.63 < 1.645: do not reject H₀.

worked.title: Two judges (two proportions, pooled)

problem.text: Judge 1 made 90 false positives in 3,000 cases; Judge 2 made 48 in 2,500. At α = 0.05, has Judge 1 made more false positives (right-tailed)?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: P₁ = P₂, H₁: P₁ > P₂.

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.text: Unpooled SE (0.004151) gives z = 2.60: same decision. The professor's doubt about the slide does not change the answer here.

worked.answer: z = 2.55 > 1.645: Judge 1 has a higher false-positive rate.

worked.title: Sports-car mileage (one-sample t, check the sign)

problem.text: A claim: mean annual mileage is 18,580 km. A sample of 10 owners has mean 17,352 and s = 2,012. A consumer firm suspects the true mean is **lower**. Test at 5% and at 1%.

steps.label: 1% level
steps.text: Critical value −2.821. −1.93 > −2.821: do not reject H₀.

steps.label: Trap
steps.text: If H₁ were μ > 18,580 (as printed on the slide), t = −1.93 could never reject (p = 0.96). Match the tail to the sign.

worked.answer: t = −1.93: reject at 5% but not at 1% (left-tailed).

worked.title: Courier packets (pooled two-sample t)

problem.text: 15 packets at the start of the month: mean 5.25 kg, variance 1.20. 10 packets at the end: mean 4.26 kg, variance 1.15. At 5%, are start-of-month packets heavier? Give the p-value and a 95% CI for the difference.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ₁ ≤ μ₂, H₁: μ₁ > μ₂ (one-tailed: "heavier").

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: One-tailed 5% critical value 1.714 < 2.23, p = 0.018: reject H₀.

steps.label: 95% CI
steps.text: 0.99 ± 2.069 × 0.4436 = (0.07, 1.91). It excludes 0, which agrees with rejecting equality.

worked.answer: t = 2.23 > 1.714 (p ≈ 0.018): packets at the start of the month are heavier.

worked.title: Trainee test scores (paired t)

problem.text: Nine trainees took an aptitude test before and after a programme. Differences d = after − before: −5, 7, 11, −8, 11, 21, 0, 9, −1. Is there an improvement at 5%?

steps.label: Critical value
steps.text: t₀.₀₅(8) = **1.860** (the slide's 1.833 is the df = 9 value).

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 1.63 < 1.860, p = 0.071: do not reject H₀. A two-tailed test (critical 2.306) also fails to reject.

worked.answer: t = 1.63 < 1.860: not enough evidence of improvement.

worked.title: Accident timing vs fatality (χ² independence, 2 × 2)

problem.text: Of 400 accidents, 280 happened in the early hours and 120 at other times. 99 accidents were fatal overall; 80 of the fatal ones were early-hours. Test at 5% whether timing and outcome are associated.

steps.label: Table
steps.text: Early: fatal 80, non-fatal 200 (total 280). Other: fatal 19, non-fatal 101 (total 120). Column totals 99 and 301.

steps.label: Expected
steps.text: E = row × column / 400: 69.3, 210.7, 29.7, 90.3. All ≥ 5, so χ² is fine.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: Critical value 3.841; 7.32 > 3.841 (p = 0.007): reject H₀. Timing and fatality are associated.

worked.answer: χ² = 7.32 > 3.841: reject independence.

worked.title: Smoking and hypertension (χ², 2 × 3)

problem.text: 180 people: hypertension yes: 21 non-smokers, 36 moderate, 30 heavy (87). No: 48, 26, 19 (93). Column totals 69, 62, 49. Test independence at 5%.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 14.46 > 5.991 (p < 0.001): reject H₀. Smoking habit and hypertension are associated.

worked.answer: χ² = 14.46 > 5.991: associated.

worked.title: Digits in a phone book (goodness of fit)

problem.text: 10,000 digits from a directory: counts for 0 to 9 are 1026, 1107, 997, 966, 1075, 933, 1107, 972, 954, 853. Test whether the digits are uniform (α = 0.05).

steps.label: H₀
steps.text: Every digit has probability 0.1. The slide takes E = 1,000 each. (The listed counts add to 9,990, not the stated 10,000; using E = 999 gives 59.41, the same decision.)

worked.answer: χ² ≈ 59.4 > 16.919: digits are not uniformly distributed.

worked.title: Bus arrivals and Poisson (χ² with an estimated parameter)

problem.text: 200 buses fall into 6 categories (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ≥5 arrivals) with O = 10, 13, 45, 49, 32, 41. Poisson probabilities with λ = 2.96 give E = 10.48, 30.90, 45.54, 44.76, 33.02, 35.30. Test at α = 0.01 whether arrivals follow a Poisson law.

steps.label: df
steps.text: k − 1 − m = 6 − 1 − 1 = **4** (λ = 2.96 was estimated from the data).

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: Critical value 13.277; 11.75 < 13.277: do not reject. A Poisson model is acceptable.

steps.label: Trap
steps.text: Using df = 5 would give critical 15.09: the same decision here, but wrong in general.

worked.answer: χ² = 11.75 < 13.28: Poisson fit is acceptable (df = 4).

worked.title: Pension plans (χ² independence, 2 × 3)

problem.text: 500 employees: Salaried 166, 86, 68 (320) for plans 1, 2, 3. Hourly 84, 64, 32 (180). Is plan choice associated with job class (α = 0.05)?

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: df = 2, critical 5.991. 4.21 < 5.991 (p = 0.12): do not reject H₀.

worked.answer: χ² = 4.21 < 5.991: no evidence of association.

worked.title: Insurance type and hospital stay: can χ² be used?

problem.text: Counts: Type 1: 42 stays ≤ 10 days, 3 stays > 10. Type 2: 18 and 7. Total 70. Can a χ² test of independence be applied?

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: The χ² approximation is unreliable. Merge categories if sensible, or use an exact test. (Computed anyway, χ² = 5.97 and df = 1, but don't trust it.)

worked.answer: No: an expected count is below 5.

worked.title: Two training programmes (two-sample t) · Mar 2026

problem.text: Program A: n = 20, mean 81, s = 9. Program B: n = 25, mean 77, s = 8. At 5%, does A give significantly higher productivity?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ_A ≤ μ_B, H₁: μ_A > μ_B (right-tailed).

steps.label: Statistic
steps.text: The key used SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) = 2.571, t = 4/2.571 = **1.56**. The pooled version gives 1.58.

steps.label: Critical value
steps.text: df = 43; one-tailed 5% critical value is about 1.68.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 1.56 < 1.68: do not reject H₀. No significant evidence that A is better.

worked.answer: t ≈ 1.56 < 1.68: not significant.

worked.title: Underfilled packets (one-sample z) · Mar 2026

problem.text: Claimed mean weight 500 g. n = 81, x̄ = 496 g, known σ = 18 g. At 5%, is the machine underfilling?

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: −2 < −1.645 (p = 0.023): reject H₀. The machine is underfilling.

worked.answer: z = −2 < −1.645: reject; underfilling.

worked.title: Paired scores and a drug claim · Feb 2026

problem.text: (a) Six students' scores before: 32, 35, 30, 33, 31, 34; after: 36, 38, 34, 37, 35, 39. Does the strategy improve scores at 5%? (b) A tool is claimed to cut diagnosis time by 20 min; 36 patients show a mean cut of 18.2 min with σ = 7.5. Evaluate the claim at 5%.

steps.label: (a) Statistic
steps.text: t = 4/(0.632/√6) = **15.5**, df = 5. One-tailed critical 2.015 (the key used 2.571, the two-tailed value). Reject H₀: the strategy helps.

steps.label: (b) Decision
steps.text: −1.44 > −1.645: do not reject. The data do not show that the reduction is below the claimed 20 minutes.

worked.answer: (a) t = 15.5: reject. (b) z = −1.44: do not reject.

worked.title: Two fertilisers (two-sample z) · May 2026

problem.text: Fertiliser A: n = 64, mean 25 kg, σ = 4. Fertiliser B: n = 81, mean 22 kg, σ = 5. Is there a significant difference at 5%?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ_A = μ_B, H₁: μ_A ≠ μ_B.

worked.answer: z = 4.01: the mean yields differ significantly.

worked.title: Vaccination in two cities (two proportions) · Feb 2026

problem.text: City A: 180 of 300 vaccinated. City B: 135 of 250. Is the proportion different at 5%?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: P₁ = P₂, H₁: P₁ ≠ P₂.

worked.answer: z = 1.42: no significant difference.

worked.title: Device type and purchase (χ²) · Mar 2026

problem.text: Mobile: 80 bought, 120 did not. Laptop: 70 and 50. Tablet: 50 and 30. Test independence at 5%.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 16.33 > 5.991 (p = 0.0003): reject. Device type and purchase are associated.

steps.label: Answer-key note
steps.text: The key writes "χ² calc = 5.991" at the end; that number is the table value.

worked.answer: χ² = 16.33 > 5.991: associated.

worked.title: Drug claim and a proportion claim · Sep 2025 / earlier batch

problem.text: (a) A drug is claimed to cut blood pressure by 15 mmHg. 25 patients: mean cut 13, s = 5. Test at 5%. (b) A drug is claimed effective in 75% of patients; 380 of 500 recovered. Test at 1%.

steps.label: (a) Decision
steps.text: Two-tailed 5% critical value ±2.064: |−2.0| < 2.064, do not reject. (A one-tailed H₁: μ < 15 would reject, critical −1.711, so say which tail you used and why.)

steps.label: (b) Decision
steps.text: |0.52| < 2.576: do not reject. The 75% claim stands.

worked.answer: (a) t = −2.0: do not reject (two-tailed). (b) z = 0.52: do not reject.

flashcards.front: What is the null hypothesis H₀?
flashcards.back: A statement of no difference or of the claim being tested, always containing an equality (=, ≤ or ≥). It is what we try to reject.

flashcards.front: What is the alternative hypothesis H₁?
flashcards.back: The strict complement of H₀ (≠, > or <). It is what we conclude if H₀ is rejected, and its sign fixes the tail.

flashcards.front: What is a z-test?
flashcards.back: Test of a mean when σ is known (or n ≥ 30). The spread is trusted, so the standard normal curve is used.

flashcards.front: What is a t-test, and how does it differ from z?
flashcards.back: Test of a mean when σ is unknown and n is small. The spread is estimated from the sample, so the fatter-tailed t curve (df = n − 1) is used and a bigger gap is needed to reject. As n grows, t becomes z.

flashcards.front: What is an unpaired (independent two-sample) t-test?
flashcards.back: Compares the means of two separate groups with no link between their members. Pooled t, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. H₀: μ₁ = μ₂.

flashcards.front: What is a paired t-test?
flashcards.back: Compares two measurements on the same subjects (before and after). Take each difference d, then do a one-mean t-test on d with H₀: μ_d = 0. df = number of pairs − 1.

flashcards.front: Which sign of H₁ gives which tail?
flashcards.back: < is left-tailed, > is right-tailed, ≠ is two-tailed.

flashcards.front: What is a Type I error?
flashcards.back: Rejecting H₀ when it is true. Its probability is α.

flashcards.front: What is a Type II error?
flashcards.back: Not rejecting H₀ when it is false. Its probability is β; power = 1 − β.

flashcards.front: What does α represent?
flashcards.back: The maximum Type I error probability you accept; it sets the rejection region (usually 0.05 or 0.01).

flashcards.front: Define the p-value.
flashcards.back: The probability, if H₀ is true, of a statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed. Reject if p ≤ α.

flashcards.front: What does "fail to reject H₀" mean?
flashcards.back: There is not enough evidence against H₀. It does not prove H₀ true (not guilty is not innocent).

flashcards.front: z cut-offs at 5%?
flashcards.back: One-tailed 1.645, two-tailed ±1.96.

flashcards.front: z cut-offs at 1%?
flashcards.back: One-tailed 2.33, two-tailed ±2.58.

flashcards.front: Why does a two-tailed test use α/2 in each tail?
flashcards.back: The total Type I error must still be α, shared between both tails, which pushes the cut-offs outwards.

flashcards.front: Statistic for one mean when σ is known?
When do you use t instead of z?
flashcards.back: σ unknown and n < 30. The statistic is (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

flashcards.front: Why use μ = K when H₀ is μ ≥ K?
flashcards.back: K is the boundary, the most conservative choice: for any larger true μ the Type I error is smaller, so it never exceeds α.

flashcards.front: Standard error for two independent means?
flashcards.back: √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), because the variances of independent sample means add.

flashcards.front: Pooled variance and df in the two-sample t-test?
flashcards.back: s_p² = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁+n₂−2), df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

flashcards.front: When is the paired t-test used, and its df?
flashcards.back: The same subjects measured twice. t = d̄/(s_d/√n) on the differences, df = n − 1 (pairs).

flashcards.front: Standard error for a proportion test?
flashcards.back: √(P₀Q₀/n), using the claimed P₀ under H₀.

flashcards.front: Pooled proportion for two proportions?
flashcards.back: p* = (x₁ + x₂)/(n₁ + n₂); z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p*q*(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)) when H₀ is P₁ = P₂.

flashcards.front: Formula and tail for chi-square?
flashcards.back: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, right-tailed only.

flashcards.front: Expected count in an r × c table and df?
flashcards.back: E = row total × column total / N. df = (r − 1)(c − 1).

flashcards.front: df for goodness of fit?
flashcards.back: k − 1 − m, where m is the number of parameters estimated from the data (Poisson with estimated λ: k − 2).

flashcards.front: Conditions for using chi-square?
flashcards.back: Counts only (not percentages), categorical data, every expected count at least 5.

flashcards.front: Which test for three or more means?
flashcards.back: One-way ANOVA (CS 10), never repeated t-tests.

flashcards.front: F-test statistic for two variances?
flashcards.back: F = s₁²/s₂² with df (n₁−1, n₂−1); right-tailed when H₁ says σ₁² > σ₂².

flashcards.front: What does the exam z-table show, and where is z?
flashcards.back: Area to the LEFT of z. z is on the edges (row = first two digits, column = second decimal); the areas are the numbers inside.

flashcards.front: How do you get the cut-off z from α for a right-tailed test?
flashcards.back: Search the inside of the table for 1 − α (0.95 for 5%), read z from the edges (1.645), and keep the plus sign.

flashcards.front: How do you get the cut-off for a left-tailed test?
flashcards.back: Find the positive cut-off the same way (search 1 − α), then make it negative. Left 5% is −1.645.

flashcards.front: How do you get a two-tailed cut-off?
flashcards.back: Split α: search 1 − α/2 (0.975 for 5%), giving ±1.96.

flashcards.front: How do you get a p-value from z with a left-area table?
flashcards.back: Look up |z| to get the left area, then tail = 1 − area. Two-tailed: double it. Valid when z is on the side H₁ points to.

flashcards.front: A right-tailed test has x̄ below the claim. What is the decision?
flashcards.back: Do not reject H₀. z is negative, p is above 0.5, and the data point away from H₁.

flashcards.front: Cut-off versus p-value: which way do you go through the table?
flashcards.back: Cut-off: start with α, search 1 − α inside the table, read z. p-value: start with z, read the area, then p = 1 − area.

flashcards.front: Where does the "1 −" come in for the cut-off, and for p?
flashcards.back: For the cut-off it comes before the lookup (search 1 − α). For p it comes after the lookup (1 − area).

flashcards.front: Can p be negative? What carries the sign?
flashcards.back: No. p is a probability between 0 and 1. The sign belongs to z and the cut-off, and shows direction (left negative, right positive).

quiz.q: A car dealership announces that the mean time for an oil change is less than 15 minutes. What is H₀?
quiz.explain: H₀ must contain the equality, and it is the complement of H₁: μ < 15, so H₀ is μ ≥ 15.

quiz.q: A study reports p = 0.03 and uses α = 0.01. What is the decision?
quiz.explain: p = 0.03 > α = 0.01, so there is not enough evidence to reject H₀.

quiz.q: "Fail to reject H₀" means…
options: The evidence is not strong enough against H₀
quiz.explain: It is a one-way test: weak evidence against H₀ is not proof for H₀ (not guilty is not innocent).

quiz.q: A Type I error is…
quiz.explain: Type I: false alarm, probability α. Type II is the miss.

quiz.q: For a two-tailed z-test at α = 0.05, the critical values are…
quiz.explain: α/2 = 0.025 in each tail, which gives ±1.96.

quiz.q: n = 15, σ is unknown, the population is roughly normal. Which statistic?
quiz.explain: σ unknown and small n: t with n − 1 = 14 df.

quiz.q: Why do we compute the statistic at μ = K when H₀ is μ ≥ K?
options: Because K is the average value in H₀
It makes the Type I error at most α for every μ allowed by H₀
It removes the need for s
quiz.explain: K is the boundary. For any larger true μ the curve shifts right and the Type I error shrinks, so α is an upper bound.

quiz.q: The same 10 patients are weighed before and after a diet. Which test?
quiz.explain: The same subjects measured twice are dependent, so use the differences.

quiz.q: A question says the average is "significantly different" from the claim. The test is…
quiz.explain: Different in either direction means H₁ uses ≠, a two-tailed test.

quiz.q: In a goodness-of-fit test of 6 categories where λ of a Poisson model was estimated from the data, df =…
Which situation breaks the rules for a χ² test?
options: An expected count of 3.57 in one cell
quiz.explain: Every expected count should be at least 5; with 3.57 the approximation is unreliable.

quiz.q: The variance of a single 0/1 observation with success probability P is…
quiz.explain: E(X²) − (E X)² = P − P² = P(1 − P) = PQ, which gives the proportion's SE √(PQ/n).

quiz.q: Sodium test: n = 44, x̄ = 925, s = 18, μ₀ = 920. Compute z.
Delivery time: n = 50, x̄ = 3.4, σ = 1.2, μ₀ = 3. Compute z.
Survival: 18 of 20 survived, H₀: P = 0.85. Compute z.
Two judges: 90/3,000 and 48/2,500. Compute the pooled proportion p*.
Device table: Laptop row total 120, "Purchased" column total 200, N = 400. Expected count?
Degrees of freedom for a 3 × 4 contingency table?
Packets: n = 81, x̄ = 496, μ₀ = 500, σ = 18. Compute z.
Device table χ² (expected 100, 100, 60, 60, 40, 40; observed 80, 120, 70, 50, 50, 30).

formulas.name: Hypotheses
formulas.formula: H₀ contains =, ≤ or ≥; H₁ is <, > or ≠
formulas.note: The sign of H₁ sets the tail.

formulas.name: Decision rule
formulas.formula: p ≤ α  ⇒  reject H₀    |    statistic beyond the critical value  ⇒  reject H₀
formulas.note: Two-tailed: p = 2 × tail area, or compare with z_{α/2}.

formulas.name: One mean, z
formulas.note: σ known, or n ≥ 30 with s in place of σ.

formulas.name: Two means, pooled t
formulas.formula: s_p² = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁+n₂−2);  t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/(s_p√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)),  df = n₁ + n₂ − 2

formulas.name: Paired t
formulas.note: d = after − before; n = number of pairs.

formulas.name: One proportion
formulas.note: Finite-population factor √((N−n)/(N−1)) is dropped when n ≪ N.

formulas.name: Two proportions
formulas.note: Pooled when H₀: P₁ = P₂. Unpooled SE: √(p̂₁q̂₁/n₁ + p̂₂q̂₂/n₂).

formulas.name: Chi-square
formulas.formula: χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E,   E = row total × column total / N
formulas.note: Right-tailed. Independence df = (r−1)(c−1). Goodness-of-fit df = k − 1 − m. Need E ≥ 5.

formulas.name: F-test (two variances)
formulas.note: Not in the CS 9 slides; asked in Sep 2025.

formulas.name: Errors
formulas.formula: α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true),  β = P(do not reject H₀ | H₀ false),  power = 1 − β

formulas.name: 5 core steps
formulas.formula: 1 H₀/H₁ and tail   2 α   3 statistic = (x̄ − μ₀)/SE   4 cut-off or p-value   5 verdict in words

formulas.name: Cut-off by tail (left-area table)
formulas.formula: Left: −z where Φ(z) = 1 − α   Right: +z where Φ(z) = 1 − α   Two: ±z where Φ(z) = 1 − α/2
formulas.note: Search the area inside the table; z is on the edges.

formulas.name: p-value by tail
formulas.formula: Right/Left: p = 1 − Φ(|z|)   Two-tailed: p = 2 × (1 − Φ(|z|))
formulas.note: Use only if z lies on the side H₁ points to; otherwise p > 0.5 and you cannot reject.
